Russian President Vladimir Putin confirmed that the next round of talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine is expected to begin next Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, with Russian state media reporting the talks would last two days. Putin said he invited members of the Russian delegation, headed by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, to a UN Security Council meeting ahead of the negotiations, Tass reported. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff previously said the parties intend to discuss security guarantees, de-escalation, humanitarian issues and further steps toward a peaceful settlement. - Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff, says he plans Cabinet changes after midterm losses Trump announced that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting Monday, while Wiles moves to the Trump political operation. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves,” Trump told reporters, saying he “wanted to make a change.” Trump said he plans to make changes to his Cabinet after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this week, telling CBS News’ 60 Minutes, “I do, yeah. Little bit,” when asked whether he plans to fire anyone, in an interview set to air Sunday. - Bomb threats target flights, media outlets in at least 5 European countries Bomb threats targeted flights, airports and media organizations in at least five European countries, prompting security inspections and evacuations, according to authorities and the media. Two aircraft departing from London and Brussels were diverted to Sofia and landed safely, while Czech police inspected nine aircraft following anonymous threats against four arrivals and five departures at Prague Airport. The French prime minister’s office said four aircraft flying over French territory received threats and all landed safely, and Copenhagen Police completed security checks at the city’s airport. items.excerpt: Today's digest 01 · Lead story 6 outlets updated 08:00 UTC # US hits Iranian air defences on Qeshm as Qatar urges a deal Trump confirmed another round of "minor" US strikes on an Iranian anti-aircraft system on Qeshm Island, after Iran said it shot down a US MQ-9 drone there. He said the US has made "a lot of progress" with Iran. Qatar's prime minister said the crisis "cannot be left unresolved" and the US remains willing to seek a solution, while officials say Iran is reviewing a Qatari plan for UN nuclear inspections that could reopen Hormuz. Al Jazeera English · 00:17 UTC Today so far as of 08:00 UTC 4 min read ## Saturday 7 November The US carried out another round of what Trump called "minor" strikes on Iran, even as mediators say Tehran is reviewing nuclear proposals and a deal may be closer than the fighting suggests. Hormuz remains closed and ships keep getting hit. In Ukraine, Russia launched its heaviest overnight barrage on Kyiv's power grid in days, while Europe and Washington differ over how to approach next week's talks in Abu Dhabi. In the US, the fallout from Tuesday's midterms continues: the Justice Department backed down in California and Trump promoted Stephen Miller. 1. 02 ### Russia fires about 30 missiles at Kyiv energy sites overnight updated 08:00 Russia-Ukraine war · 685 developments Russia fired about 30 missiles at energy and industrial sites in Kyiv and its region, including the Trypillia power plant, and damaged the Northern Bridge. Zhytomyr and Chernihiv lost power, Kyiv has heating, water and power problems, and at least five people were injured, including a 14-year-old. Zelensky says every Ukrainian power plant has been damaged. Ukraine hit the Saratov refinery and the Proton-Electrotex plant in Orel. The toll from the Nov 2 Komyshuvakha strike rose to 55. video From The Kyiv Independent, Suspilne, Mash, Топор Live and 1 more 2. 03 ### Europe says Putin must end war first as Abu Dhabi talks near updated 08:00 Russia-Ukraine peace talks prospects · 279 developments Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to hold trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, confirmed by Putin, with Umerov leading Ukraine's delegation. Zelensky rejects a US-floated new European security deal with Russia ("no Yalta 2") and says Ukraine won't give up Donbas, and the EU demands a seat. European allies insist Putin must end the war before Russia's concerns are discussed, risking a split with Washington. Trump promises a "big beautiful deal" that he says will affect all of Europe. From The Japan Times, Топор Live 3. 04 ### Justice Department drops California ballot suit after Republican midterm losses added 04:00 US midterms early voting surge · 103 developments Democrats won the US Senate and House and a majority of governorships, though Mississippi's Senate race is still being counted. Trump accepts the results but calls the elections "crooked". The Justice Department moved to dismiss its own suit over up to 20,000 California ballots it suspected went to noncitizens. Voters rejected data-centre projects in 40 of 41 local measures, and tech stocks had their worst day since 2020 on fears of tougher AI rules. From Associated Press, Al Jazeera ... ### Eisenkot poised for mandate as Haredi draft shift reshapes coalition maths added 04:00 Israel's October election campaign · 248 developments Eisenkot has recommendations from 67 of 120 MKs against 46 for Netanyahu and is poised to get the mandate from Herzog, who names his pick on Sunday. The new Knesset is sworn in on Nov 10. United Torah Judaism welcomed Lieberman's softer line on Haredi conscription but withheld endorsement of Netanyahu, and Shas, which holds the decisive 61st seat, remains reluctant. Eisenkot signals readiness for a minority government. From Haaretz ... ### Settlers beat Palestinian unconscious in Masafer Yatta; Herzog calls West Bank "explosive" updated 08:00 West Bank settler violence and raids · 213 developments Settlers were filmed beating a Palestinian man unconscious with clubs overnight in a Masafer Yatta hamlet south of Hebron; no arrests were made. Palestinian officials counted 20 attacks on olive pickers on Friday, and the UN says 377 settler attacks on the olive harvest since September are a record since 2006. Settlers moved into eight houses outside Jericho, displacing dozens. Israel closed Hebron's Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians. Herzog warned Netanyahu the West Bank is "highly explosive". From The Times of Israel, Middle East Eye ... ### Eleven ships attacked around Hormuz in a week, three sunk added 04:00 Attack on ship near Oman · 15 developments UKMTO counted 11 attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Gulf in the week to Nov 4: eight in Hormuz, three in the Gulf. One dhow crew member was killed and a Panama-flagged supply vessel sank. The IRGC said two more tankers hit mines on Friday, and South Korea is sending a military mission towards Hormuz.

items.title: Musalem says inflation concern persists, expectations anchored
items.excerpt: Last updated: 7 November 2026 03:04 Enver Adıgüzel - Editor and Publisher 9 minutes ago St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said people remain concerned about inflation at the current level. He said inflation expectations remain anchored. The Fed, he said, must return inflation to 2% on a timely basis. Contents - Energy shocks and AI spending - Communication and policy transmission ## Energy shocks and AI spending Musalem attributed the current excess inflation to energy shocks and the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. He said consumption and investment are growing fast on an optimistic outlook. He argued that AI will bring much higher productivity, and that data center construction is adding to strong demand. Musalem’s remarks point to demand as well as energy costs as the source of the pressure. ## Communication and policy transmission Musalem said clear Fed communication helps policy move through the economy more smoothly. The US federal funds rate stood at 3.88 percent in force since 5 November, by our market data as of 03:11 GMT on 7 November. US annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September, near its 31-day high.

items.title: Americans feel a little better, and expect less inflation | How the World Works
items.excerpt: How the World Works · 7 Nov 2026 Key takeaways - US consumer sentiment rose to 51.0 in early November and year-ahead inflation expectations fell to 4.3% from 4.7%. - Expectations matter because people act on them, in pay demands, pricing and spending. - Long-run expectations, at 3.4%, are still well above the Fed's 2% target, so one good month is not enough. 51.0 Consumer sentiment, Nov (prelim.) 4.3% Year-ahead inflation expected (was 4.7%) 3.4% Long-run inflation expected (was 3.5%) 3.4% Year-ahead expectation in February ## What happened The University of Michigan's index of US consumer sentiment rose to 51.0 in its preliminary November reading, published on 6 November, from 48.0 in October. Economists had expected no change. Both parts of the index improved: views of current conditions rose to 51.0 from 46.7, and expectations to 50.9 from 48.8. Sentiment is still about 10% below its level in February, before the oil shock. The inflation households expect also eased. Over the next year, they expect prices to rise 4.3%, down from 4.7% in October and the lowest since August. Over the long run, five to ten years ahead, they expect 3.4%, down from 3.5%. In February, year-ahead expectations were 3.4%. ## Why expectations matter Inflation is partly self-fulfilling. If workers expect prices to rise 4% next year, they ask for bigger pay rises; if firms expect their costs to rise, they raise prices sooner. Both make the expected inflation more likely to happen. That is why central banks watch surveys like this one closely, especially the long-run measure: a rise there would suggest people have stopped believing inflation will return to target. Two weeks ago, these expectations were at a five-month high (our story). The fall in oil prices may have helped: fuel is the price households see most often, and it shapes what they expect. ## What it means for the Fed For the Federal Reserve, it is a mixed week. October's jobs report was strong, with 165,000 new jobs, which argues for a rate rise in December. Easing inflation expectations argue for patience. Long-run expectations of 3.4% are still well above the 2% target, and above the 2.8% to 3.2% range seen in 2024. ... - University of Michigan, Surveys of Consumers, preliminary November 2026 (6 November 2026), as reported by Verified Investing and IndexBox

items.title: Fed’s Williams says energy prices have already peaked despite new Iran fighting | Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide
items.excerpt: in World Economy News 11/07/2026 Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said today he does not expect a sustained rise in energy prices for the rest of the year, despite renewed conflict in the Middle East. Williams told a conference at his bank that market expectations for oil prices to decline over the next six to 12 months remain reasonable. He said the fundamentals suggest energy prices are likely around their peak and should come down over time. The Fed official said inflation remains “far too high” and that monetary policy is focused on how energy prices impact inflation. Williams added that artificial intelligence investment is currently driving inflation, though he expects AI to become a positive supply shock in the longer term. His base case sees broader AI use boosting productivity. Williams said the Fed is actively debating scenarios around inflation and remains committed to bringing inflation back to 2%. He stressed the importance of looking at underlying inflation factors rather than just specific measures, noting that government technical changes could better reconcile differences between PCE inflation and CPI. The New York Fed president said monetary policy needs to remain data dependent. He described the labor market as very stable. Williams noted that uncertainty remains about the longer-term neutral rate and that the Fed minutes captured a “collective reaction function.”

items.excerpt: The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state. According to the order, Houston police will contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence, according to the Reuters news agency. Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, and that the move was meant to reduce fear and anxiety across the city. “Elections matter,” Whitmire told reporters. “I do this to begin a healing process,” he said, adding he hoped his executive order would become a model for other Texas cities. Joining Whitmire at the news conference, Houston Police ⁠Chief J Noe Diaz said he supported the change and that his department had already begun to implement the new policy. Under the new rules, people stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to ICE simply because they have an administrative immigration warrant. The decision reverses a policy Whitmire put in place in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott. Abbott had threatened to withdraw about $110m in state public safety grants, arguing that a city council ordinance limiting police contact with ICE breached Senate Bill 4, a 2017 state law that bars local police from restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued the mayor, the city council and the police chief over the ordinance. “We’re taking an interpretation of the law today, working with the newly elected members of the state leadership, in implementing this policy,” Whitmire told reporters. “We don’t want people to worry about ⁠their workers, their family members, their students.” The issue has drawn intense scrutiny in Houston. The Houston Chronicle found that city police contacted ICE at least 107 times in the first eight months of 2025, compared with nine times in the whole of 2024. In July, an ICE agent shot dead Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a longtime Houston resident. FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, called the order a victory for the city but said it was long overdue. “Today Houston won. Today our community can breathe easier,” FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said in a statement to KPRC. Whitmire said he expected Houston’s approach to become a model for other cities. In Austin, Mayor Kirk Watson asked city officials on Friday to revise their own policy on ICE warrants.

items.title: AP News in Brief at 12:04 a.m. EST | 10tv.com
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year. Miller, long a member of Trump’s tight inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy. The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday's midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president's executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump's presidency. Wiles gave Trump her resignation Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told The Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization. Trump on Friday night denied that he made the change because he was unhappy with his team after the deep losses his party suffered. ... WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday. Jason Reding Quiñones' resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues. The Justice Department’s top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department's Civil Rights Division, also announced her departure. Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president. His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

(AP) — Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old father of Prince Harry’s wife Meghan, has been arrested by federal agents in Florida and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material in California. Thomas Markle was released after a court appearance in Tampa. Authorities say a search of storage units in the Los Angeles area turned up dozens of items. Meghan Markle had recently said she's “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images were found at her father’s former home in the Philippines. 25 years after 'Britney,' 5 new Britney Spears songs showcase a pop icon at a transformative moment NEW YORK (AP) — Britney Spears' 2001 self-titled album ‘Britney' marked a pivotal moment in her career. At 19, she was already a global icon, transitioning from teen pop to a more mature sound. The album, certified quadruple platinum, showcased her evolution with hits like “I'm a Slave 4 U.” On Friday, Legacy Recordings releases the “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition).” It features five previously unreleased tracks and two new remixes. These songs add depth to her legacy, reflecting themes of autonomy and self-definition. Fans can revisit the album, exploring its impact and Spears’ journey from adolescence to adulthood. Awkwafina digs into her culinary roots to try something a little crazy: Open a restaurant NEW YORK (AP) — Awkwafina has taken a surprising turn in her career by diving into the culinary world. Her new Apple TV series, “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” follows her journey from a novice cook to opening her own restaurant. The show, premiering Friday, captures her learning experiences, from making stir-fry to mastering Peking duck. Awkwafina was born Nora Lum and comes from a family with a rich restaurant history. They opened the New York City eatery Lum's. Her journey reconnects her with her roots and honors her family. The series also highlights a trend of Asian Americans returning to the restaurant industry, defying their parents' expectations. In 'Being Heumann,' Siân Heder and Ruth Madeley channel the spirit of a disability rights pioneer NEW YORK (AP) — Siân Heder's follow-up to the best picture-winning “CODA” chronicles the disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann. Heumann died at the age of 75 in 2023 while Heder was developing the movie with her. She resolved to push on with the project to honor Heumann and try to bring some of her accessibility gains to the movie industry. Characters with disabilities remain extremely uncommon in Hollywood productions, and big-screen biopics like “Being Heumann” are even more seldom. “Being Heumann,” starring Ruth Madeley as Heumann, features the largest ensemble ever of performers with disabilities. Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio dies at 52 SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio has died in Santiago, Chile, at 52. His family announced his death Friday on Instagram, citing health reasons but not specifying the cause. Lelio was known for his groundbreaking film “A Fantastic Woman,” which portrayed a transgender woman and won the Academy Award for best international film. It was Chile's second Oscar win. Lelio’s other works include "Gloria," "The Wonder," and “Disobedience.” He had begun filming “Poeta Chileno” in September. Born in Argentina, Lelio moved to Chile at age two and studied at the ... Dolly Parton's manager moves to drop complaint accusing late singer's nephew of threatening estate Dolly Parton’s longtime manager has moved to drop a complaint that accused the late singer’s nephew of threatening her estate and its employees. She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September. A hearing, pushed several times over the course of a month, was slated for next Tuesday. A very brief filing in a Tennessee court Thursday gives no reason why the complaint is being withdrawn. 'ER' and 'The Pitt' are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court finds LOS ANGELES (AP) — A California appeals court has found enough similarity between “ER” and “The Pitt” for a lawsuit by Michael Crichton's widow to proceed. The court ruled that the trial judge was correct to reject Warner Bros. Television's motion to dismiss. Both shows star Noah Wyle as an emergency room doctor and focus on the healthcare system. The lawsuit argues “The Pitt” is an unauthorized “ER” reboot. Crichton had a contract preventing any “ER” spinoffs without his consent. The court dismissed claims against Wyle and others, finding no evidence they interfered with Crichton's contract.
